--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Dog' slide-number: true css: ../../custom.css lang: en --- ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 160%;"}
Occupancy models:
covariates and prediction
::: {style="font-size: 70%;"} WILD(FISH) 8390
Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
:::
# Overview {visibility="hidden"} ## Overview ::: {style="font-size: 90%;"} Explaining variation in occupancy and detection probability with covariates is central to reliable prediction and scientific investigation.

::: {.fragment} In static occupancy models, there are two types of covariates: - [Site covariates]{style="color: blue;"} vary among sites but not among occasions. - [Observation covariates]{style="color: Coral;"} may vary among sites and occasions :::
::: {.fragment} In both cases, covariates can be continuous or categorical. ::: ::: {.fragment} Observation covariates [cannot](style="color: red;") be used to describe variation in occupancy because occupancy is assumed to be constant over time.
::: ::: ## Covariates ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} State model $$ \small \begin{gather*} \mathrm{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} + \beta_2 {\color{blue} x_{i2}} + \cdots \\ z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi_i) \end{gather*} $$ Observation model $$ \small \begin{gather*} \mathrm{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 {\color{blue} x_{i1}} + \alpha_2 {\color{Coral} w_{ij}} + \cdots \\ y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_i\times p_{ij}) \end{gather*} $$ $\color{blue} x_1$ and $\color{blue} x_2$ are site covariates.
Examples: elevation, forest cover, distance to water. $\color{Coral} w$ is an observation covariate.
Examples: time of day, observer, wind. ::: # Simulation {visibility="hidden"} ## Simulation ::: {style="font-size: 78%;"} Two continuous covariates and one categorical covariate with 2 levels. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nSites <- 200; nVisits <- 4; set.seed(83) # Make it reproducible elev <- rnorm(nSites,5000,500) # Site covariate (continuous) forest <- rnorm(nSites,100,10) # Another continuous site covariate temp <- matrix(sample(c("Cold", "Hot"), size=nSites*nVisits, replace=TRUE), nrow=nSites, ncol=nVisits) # Categorical obs covar tempHot <- ifelse(temp=="Hot", 1, 0) # Dummy variable ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} Coefficients, $\psi$, and $p$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beta0 <- 5; beta1 <- -0.001; beta2 <- 0 psi <- plogis(beta0 + beta1*elev + beta2*forest) alpha0 <- -6.5; alpha1 <- 0.001; alpha2 <- 2 p <- plogis(alpha0 + alpha1*elev + alpha2*tempHot) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Simulate occupancy and detection data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- rbinom(nSites, size=1, psi) ## pres/absence y <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=nVisits) for(i in 1:nSites) { y[i,] <- rbinom(nVisits, size=1, prob=z[i]*p[i,]) } ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Prediction in 'unmarked' ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/sim-sitch-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: Expect problems if you ignore imperfect detection in this case.
## Simulated data ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='40%'} Observations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y[1:20,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 0 1 1 1 [2,] 1 0 1 1 [3,] 0 0 0 1 [4,] 0 0 0 0 [5,] 0 0 0 0 [6,] 0 0 0 1 [7,] 0 0 0 0 [8,] 0 0 0 0 [9,] 0 0 0 0 [10,] 0 0 0 0 [11,] 1 0 1 1 [12,] 0 0 0 0 [13,] 0 0 0 0 [14,] 0 0 0 0 [15,] 0 0 0 0 [16,] 0 0 0 0 [17,] 0 0 0 0 [18,] 0 0 0 1 [19,] 0 0 0 0 [20,] 0 0 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='5%'} ::: ::: {.column width='55%'} ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} Summary stats
Detections at each site
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} siteDets <- rowSums(y) # Dets at each site table(siteDets) # Frequency ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` siteDets 0 1 2 3 4 127 34 19 18 2 ``` ::: ::: Proportion of sites known to be occupied
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} naiveOccupancy <- sum(siteDets>0)/nSites naiveOccupancy ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.365 ``` ::: ::: Actual occupancy
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(z) / nSites ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.44 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Prediction {visibility="hidden"} ## Prepare data in 'unmarked' Notice the two new arguments `siteCovs` and `obsCovs`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(elev,forest), obsCovs=list(temp=temp)) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(umf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unmarkedFrame Object 200 sites Maximum number of observations per site: 4 Mean number of observations per site: 4 Sites with at least one detection: 73 Tabulation of y observations: 0 1 666 134 Site-level covariates: elev forest Min. :3419 Min. : 69.24 1st Qu.:4768 1st Qu.: 94.01 Median :5040 Median :100.14 Mean :5042 Mean :100.14 3rd Qu.:5376 3rd Qu.:107.03 Max. :6253 Max. :128.59 Observation-level covariates: temp Cold:424 Hot :376 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Standardizing ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} It's almost always a good idea to standardize [continuous]{style="color: red;"} covariates. Standardizing involves subtracting the mean and then dividing by the standard deviation.^[You can use the R function `scale` but it's important to know how to do it yourself] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean.elev <- mean(elev); mean.forest <- mean(forest) sd.elev <- sd(elev); sd.forest <- sd(forest) elev_s <- (elev-mean.elev)/sd.elev forest_s <- (forest-mean.forest)/sd.forest siteCovs(umf)$elev_s <- elev_s siteCovs(umf)$forest_s <- forest_s ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} Standardizing makes it easier to find the maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs) and it facilitates comparison of estimates.
We just have to remember to back-transform covariates when graphing predictions. ::: ::: ## Fit the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fm <- occu(~elev_s+temp ~elev_s+forest_s, umf) # Standardized covariates fm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: occu(formula = ~elev_s + temp ~ elev_s + forest_s, data = umf) Occupancy (logit-scale): Estimate SE z P(>|z|) (Intercept) -0.284 0.177 -1.605 0.1084 elev_s -0.436 0.184 -2.377 0.0174 forest_s 0.126 0.168 0.751 0.4526 Detection (logit-scale): Estimate SE z P(>|z|) (Intercept) -1.207 0.203 -5.96 2.56e-09 elev_s 0.569 0.133 4.27 1.97e-05 tempHot 1.634 0.261 6.25 4.03e-10 AIC: 596.8205 Number of sites: 200 ``` ::: ::: ## Prediction in 'unmarked' ::: {style="font-size: 90%;"} Create a data frame with prediction covariates. We'll let elevation vary while holding the other two covariates constant. Important that we predict using the standardized covariates. We can still graph on the original scales. ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred.data <- data.frame(elev_s=seq(from=-3, to=3, length=50), forest_s=0, temp='Hot') # Standardized pred.data$elev <- pred.data$elev_s*sd.elev+mean.elev # Orig scale pred.data$forest <- pred.data$forest_s*sd.forest+mean.forest ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Get predictions of $\psi$ for each row of prediction data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} psi.pred <- predict(fm, newdata=pred.data, type='state', append=TRUE) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Get predictions of $p$ for each row of prediction data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p.pred <- predict(fm, newdata=pred.data, type='det', append=TRUE) ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Prediction in 'unmarked' View $\psi$ predictions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(head(psi.pred, n=4), digits=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Predicted SE lower upper elev_s forest_s temp elev forest 1 0.74 0.12 0.46 0.90 -3.0 0 Hot 3489 100 2 0.73 0.12 0.46 0.89 -2.9 0 Hot 3552 100 3 0.71 0.11 0.45 0.88 -2.8 0 Hot 3616 100 4 0.70 0.11 0.45 0.87 -2.6 0 Hot 3679 100 ``` ::: ::: View $p$ predictions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(head(p.pred, n=4), digits=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Predicted SE lower upper elev_s forest_s temp elev forest 1 0.22 0.073 0.11 0.39 -3.0 0 Hot 3489 100 2 0.23 0.073 0.12 0.40 -2.9 0 Hot 3552 100 3 0.24 0.073 0.13 0.41 -2.8 0 Hot 3616 100 4 0.26 0.073 0.14 0.42 -2.6 0 Hot 3679 100 ``` ::: ::: ## Standardized elevation ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mai=c(0.9,0.9,0.1,0.1)) plot(Predicted ~ elev_s, psi.pred, type="l", ylab="Occurrence probability", col="blue", xlab="Elevation (standardized)", ylim=0:1) lines(lower ~ elev_s, psi.pred, col="grey"); lines(upper ~ elev_s, psi.pred, col="grey") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/pred-psi1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ::: ## Elevation on original scale ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mai=c(0.9,0.9,0.1,0.1)) plot(Predicted ~ elev, psi.pred, type="l", ylab="Occurrence probability", col="blue", xlab="Elevation (original scale)", ylim=0:1) lines(lower ~ elev, psi.pred, col="grey"); lines(upper ~ elev, psi.pred, col="grey") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/pred-psi1s-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ::: ## Estimated vs actual occupancy ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/psi-actual-est-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## The BUGS model
[occupancy-model-covs.jag](occupancy-model-covs.jag)
::: {.cell code-block-height='650px'} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { # Priors for occupancy coefficients beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) # 0.5 is 1/variance beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) beta2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) # Priors for detection coefficients alpha0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) alpha1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) alpha2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.5) for(i in 1:nSites) { logit(psi[i]) <- beta0 + beta1*elev[i] + beta2*forest[i] z[i] ~ dbern(psi[i]) # Latent presence/absence for(j in 1:nOccasions) { logit(p[i,j]) <- alpha0 + alpha1*elev[i] + alpha2*tempHot[i,j] y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i]*p[i,j]) # Data } } sitesOccupied <- sum(z) } ``` ::: ::: ## Data, inits, and parameters Put data in a named list ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data <- list(y=y, elev=elev_s, forest=forest_s, tempHot=tempHot, nSites=nSites, nOccasions=nVisits) ``` ::: Initial values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.inits <- function() { list(beta0=rnorm(1), alpha0=rnorm(1), z=rep(1, nSites)) } ``` ::: Parameters to monitor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.pars <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "alpha0", "alpha1", "alpha2", "sitesOccupied") ``` ::: ## MCMC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(jagsUI); library(coda) jags.post.samples <- jags.basic(data=jags.data, inits=jags.inits, parameters.to.save=jags.pars, model.file="occupancy-model-covs.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Processing function input....... Done. Beginning parallel processing using 3 cores. Console output will be suppressed. Parallel processing completed. MCMC took 0.073 minutes. ``` ::: ::: ## Summarize output ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(jags.post.samples) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Iterations = 101:2100 Thinning interval = 1 Number of chains = 3 Sample size per chain = 2000 1. Empirical mean and standard deviation for each variable, plus standard error of the mean: Mean SD Naive SE Time-series SE alpha0 -1.1665 0.2020 0.002608 0.006444 alpha1 0.5660 0.1356 0.001751 0.002778 alpha2 1.5460 0.2562 0.003308 0.007300 beta0 -0.2605 0.1813 0.002341 0.004201 beta1 -0.4481 0.1914 0.002471 0.004197 beta2 0.1315 0.1699 0.002193 0.003329 sitesOccupied 87.4655 5.0831 0.065622 0.140707 2. Quantiles for each variable: 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% alpha0 -1.5695 -1.30153 -1.1630 -1.0304 -0.77441 alpha1 0.2994 0.47222 0.5642 0.6561 0.83835 alpha2 1.0521 1.37589 1.5479 1.7147 2.05739 beta0 -0.6090 -0.38581 -0.2620 -0.1393 0.10470 beta1 -0.8449 -0.57349 -0.4386 -0.3149 -0.09501 beta2 -0.2035 0.01856 0.1292 0.2455 0.46913 sitesOccupied 79.0000 84.00000 87.0000 91.0000 98.00000 ``` ::: ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/bugs-plot1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/bugs-plot2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Bayesian prediction Every MCMC iteration represents a sample from the posterior distribution.
Each sample of the occupancy and detection coefficients can be used to make a prediction.
The collection of predictions can be used to summarize the posterior predictive distribution.
We will look at the distribution of prediction lines. ## Bayesian prediction ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} First, extract the $\psi$ coefficients ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} psi.coef.post <- as.matrix(jags.post.samples[,c("beta0","beta1","beta2")]) head(psi.coef.post, n=4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` beta0 beta1 beta2 [1,] 0.03917272 -0.6438042 0.01456167 [2,] -0.05849979 -0.4680823 -0.01976281 [3,] 0.14814125 -0.4031580 -0.05574820 [4,] -0.10849216 -0.5924015 0.05711385 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Create prediction matrix, one row for each MCMC iteration. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n.iter <- nrow(psi.coef.post) psi.post.pred <- matrix(NA, nrow=n.iter, ncol=nrow(pred.data)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Predict $\psi$ for each MCMC iteration. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for(i in 1:n.iter) { psi.post.pred[i,] <- plogis(psi.coef.post[i,"beta0"] + psi.coef.post[i,"beta1"]*pred.data$elev_s) } ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Bayesian prediction Prediction line for first posterior sample ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(pred.data$elev, psi.post.pred[1,], type="l", xlab="Elevation", ylab="Occurrence probability", ylim=c(0, 1), col=gray(0.8)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/psi-pred1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Bayesian prediction All samples from the posterior predictive distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} for(i in 1:n.iter) { lines(pred.data$elev, psi.post.pred[i,], col=gray(0.8)) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/psi-pred-post-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Bayesian prediction Now with posterior mean and 95\% CI ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pred.post.mean <- colMeans(psi.post.pred) pred.post.lower <- apply(psi.post.pred, 2, quantile, prob=0.025) pred.post.upper <- apply(psi.post.pred, 2, quantile, prob=0.975) lines(pred.data$elev, pred.post.mean, col="blue") lines(pred.data$elev, pred.post.lower, col="blue", lty=2) lines(pred.data$elev, pred.post.upper, col="blue", lty=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyII_files/figure-revealjs/psi-pred-post-meanCI-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Summary of static occupancy models ::: {style="font-size: 65%;"} Assumptions are made explicit by the model description, but it's worth emphasizing that: * Occupancy is assumed to remain constant at each site during the sampling period. * The definition of a 'site' is critical, but can difficult in some situations, such as in camera studies. * Abundance is assumed to be unimportant. * Observations are assumed to be independent, conditional on latent variables and covariates. ::: {.fragment} These assumptions can be relaxed if we have enough data. * Dynamic occupancy models - Occupancy evolves as a function of local colonization and extinction. * $N$-mixture models - Focus is on local abundance, rather than presence/absence. ::: ::: {.fragment}
We'll talk more about design issues later.
::: ::: # Assignment {visibility="hidden"} ## Assignment ::: {style="font-size: 75%;"} Create a self-contained R script or Rmarkdown/Quarto file to do the following: 1. Fit an occupancy model in 'unmarked' to the Ruffed Grouse data (`"grouse_data.csv"`). Use all three covariates, with elevation and forest cover affecting occupancy and day of the year affecting detection probability. * Response: `grouse1, grouse2, grouse3` * Site covs: Elevation (`elev`), forest cover (`fc`) * Obs cov: Day of the year (`doy.1, doy.2, doy.3`) 2. Make one prediction graph for occupancy and one for detection. 3. Create the same graphs as above, but using Bayesian methods.
Upload your .R, .Rmd, or .qmd file to ELC by 5:00pm on Tuesday.
:::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
